title: Fairchild Republic A-10 Thunderbolt II
description: American close air support attack aircraft
wiki_lead:
The Fairchild Republic A-10 Thunderbolt II, also widely known by the nickname Warthog, is a single-seat, twin-turbofan, straight-wing, subsonic attack aircraft developed by Fairchild Republic for the United States Air Force (USAF). In service since 1977, it is named after the Republic P-47 Thunderbolt strike-fighter of World War II, but is commonly referred to as the "Warthog". The A-10 was designed to provide close air support (CAS) to ground troops by attacking enemy armored vehicles, tanks, and other ground forces; it is the only production-built aircraft designed solely for CAS to have served with the U.S. Air Force. Its secondary missions include combat search and rescue, and to direct other aircraft in attacks on ground targets, a role called forward air controller (FAC)-airborne; aircraft used primarily in this role are designated OA-10.  It also performs reconnaissance, air interdiction, and maritime surface warfare missions.
The A-10 was intended to improve on the performance and firepower of the Douglas A-1 Skyraider. The Thunderbolt II's airframe was designed around the high-power 30 mm GAU-8 Avenger rotary autocannon. The airframe was designed for durability, with measures such as 1,200 pounds (540 kg) of titanium armor to protect the cockpit and aircraft systems, enabling it to absorb damage and continue flying. Its ability to take off and land from relatively short and unpaved runways permits operation from airstrips close to the front lines, and its simple design enables maintenance with minimal facilities.
It served in Operation Urgent Fury in Grenada, the Gulf War (Operation Desert Storm), the Yugoslav Wars, war in Afghanistan, the Iraq War, in the conflict against the Islamic State in the Middle East, Operation Odyssey Dawn in Libya, and the 2026 Iran war.
The A-10A single-seat variant was the only version produced, though one pre-production airframe was modified into the YA-10B twin-seat prototype to test an all-weather night-capable version. In 2005, a program was started to upgrade the remaining A-10A aircraft to the A-10C configuration, with modern avionics for use with precision weaponry. The U.S. Air Force had stated the Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II would replace the A-10 as it entered service, but this remains highly contentious within the USAF and in political circles. The USAF gained congressional permission to start retiring A-10s in 2023, but further retirements were paused until the USAF can demonstrate that the A-10's close-air-support capabilities can be replaced.

Development


Background

The development of conventionally armed attack aircraft in the United States stagnated after World War II, as design efforts for tactical aircraft focused on the delivery of nuclear weapons using high-speed designs such as the McDonnell F-101 Voodoo and Republic F-105 Thunderchief. grok_lead: The Fairchild Republic A-10 Thunderbolt II is a twin-turbofan, straight-wing, single-seat close air support aircraft developed specifically for the United States Air Force to destroy enemy armored vehicles and provide direct support to ground troops in contested environments. Designed around the GAU-8/A Avenger 30 mm rotary cannon âa seven-barrel Gatling gun optimized for firing armor-piercing depleted uranium projectiles at rates up to 3,900 rounds per minuteâthe A-10 emphasizes durability, low-speed handling, and extended loiter time over speed or stealth. Its airframe incorporates a titanium-reinforced cockpit bathtub weighing approximately 1,200 pounds to shield the pilot from small-arms fire and shrapnel, along with redundant flight controls and engines positioned aft to minimize vulnerability to ground fire. First flying in May 1972 and achieving initial operational capability in 1977, the A-10 has flown over 8,000 combat sorties in operations such as Desert Storm, where it achieved a 95.7% mission-capable rate and inflicted heavy losses on Iraqi armor through precision low-level attacks, demonstrating causal effectiveness in tank destruction far exceeding multirole alternatives in similar roles. Subsequent deployments in the Balkans, Afghanistan, and Iraq further validated its survivability, with only seven total aircraft losses across thousands of missions despite routine exposure to man-portable air-defense systems and anti-aircraft artillery, underscoring the empirical superiority of its purpose-built design for close air support over generalized fighter platforms. Despite institutional Air Force preferences for retiring the type in favor of stealth-oriented aircraft since the 1990sâoften prioritizing high-altitude precision strikes that empirical data shows less effectively neutralize immediate ground threatsâthe A-10's retention through congressional intervention reflects ground force advocacy grounded in observed combat utility rather than abstract doctrinal shifts. Upgrades to the A-10C variant, including digital cockpits and precision-guided munitions integration completed by 2007, have extended its relevance into modern networked warfare while preserving core kinetic advantages. In April 2026, the USAF announced that the A-10C would remain in service at least until 2030.
